results.snippet:
## What are customer unmet needs?

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. It allows them to innovate and design solutions that align with what customers actually experience day to day. [...] ## Frequently asked questions

What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.
 Five research methods work well for uncovering unmet needs: generative research, digital ethnography, customer journey mapping, diary studies, and in-home usage tests (iHUTs).
 A multi-method approach almost always produces richer findings than any single method alone. Initial fieldwork can feed into follow-up interviews and focus groups for deeper exploration.

According to Sensor Tower data, in 2022, over 70% of top-grossing mobile games were published by indie developers or small teams, highlighting the shift from traditional publishers to grassroots innovation. Notably, the rise of user-generated content (UGC) platforms powered by mobile gaming engines fosters a participatory environment, where players are also creators, significantly increasing engagement and longevity. ## The Role of Indie Titles in Industry Growth. Emerging indie titles often differentiate themselves through unique art styles and narrative depth, appealing to niche markets that feel underserved by mainstream AAA titles. Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.
 Five research methods work well for uncovering unmet needs: generative research, digital ethnography, customer journey mapping, diary studies, and in-home usage tests (iHUTs).
 A multi-method approach almost always produces richer findings than any single method alone. Initial fieldwork can feed into follow-up interviews and focus groups for deeper exploration.

## What are customer unmet needs?

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. It allows them to innovate and design solutions that align with what customers actually experience day to day. [...] ## Frequently asked questions

What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.
 Five research methods work well for uncovering unmet needs: generative research, digital ethnography, customer journey mapping, diary studies, and in-home usage tests (iHUTs).
 A multi-method approach almost always produces richer findings than any single method alone. Initial fieldwork can feed into follow-up interviews and focus groups for deeper exploration.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. ## What are customer unmet needs?

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. It allows them to innovate and design solutions that align with what customers actually experience day to day. [...] ## Frequently asked questions

What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.
 Five research methods work well for uncovering unmet needs: generative research, digital ethnography, customer journey mapping, diary studies, and in-home usage tests (iHUTs).
 A multi-method approach almost always produces richer findings than any single method alone. Initial fieldwork can feed into follow-up interviews and focus groups for deeper exploration.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

results.snippet:
# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

## What are customer unmet needs?

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. It allows them to innovate and design solutions that align with what customers actually experience day to day. [...] ## Frequently asked questions

What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both.

Title: Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. Long-Term Institutional Adoption
# Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. The October 2025 liquidity crisis exposed deep flaws in the crypto ecosystem. Regulatory shifts in Asia, coupled with attacks on decentralized protocols, triggered a cascade of liquidations. Markets fragmented across exchanges, with no cross-venue arbitrage to stabilize prices during volatility. Ownership concentration among whales and early investors exacerbated panic selling, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of price drops and forced liquidations. Unlike traditional markets, crypto lacks robust derivatives or insurance mechanisms to absorb shocks. This fragility was compounded by off-chain settlement processes and operational risks tied to decentralized infrastructure according to analysis. Data from CoinLaw.io reveals that 78% of institutional investors now employ formal risk management frameworks, with 53% conducting liquidity stress tests-a stark contrast to 2023, when only 54% had such protocols. ### Institutional Adoption: A Counterweight to Chaos. Despite these risks, institutional participation has introduced stabilizing forces. By 2025, 59% of surveyed institutions allocated at least 10% of their portfolios to digital assets, a shift from speculative bets to strategic integration. Infrastructure innovations are addressing liquidity gaps. The impact of institutional adoption is evident in Bitcoin's reduced volatility. Annualized volatility dropped by 75% by mid-2025, driven by deeper liquidity and a "strong hands" effect, where large investors resist panic selling. ### The Path Forward: Balancing Risks and Resilience. While institutional adoption mitigates some risks, challenges persist. Cybersecurity threats remain unaddressed, and the pro-cyclical nature of crypto liquidity ensures future shocks. However, the market's trajectory suggests a path toward resilience. By 2035, the crypto market is projected to grow from $3.7 billion to $12.1 billion at a 12.6% CAGR, driven by institutional infrastructure and DeFi innovation. Exchange platforms, now accounting for 38.6% of market revenue, are integrating real-time order matching and API-based systems to bolster trust. The crypto market's resilience hinges on its ability to reconcile structural risks with institutional adoption. While liquidity shocks like the October 2025 crash underscore inherent fragility, the rise of institutional-grade infrastructure and risk management frameworks signals a maturing ecosystem. Investors must navigate this duality: embracing the long-term potential of crypto while hedging against its cyclical vulnerabilities.

## What are customer unmet needs?

Unmet needs are the wants and desires of customers that existing products or services don't fulfil. They're often surfaced through market research, customer feedback, and user research, and can range from minor inconveniences to major pain points.

These needs may come from a lack of features, poor user experience, high cost, or simply a gap in the market. Identifying and addressing them is essential for businesses to remain competitive. It allows them to innovate and design solutions that align with what customers actually experience day to day. [...] ## Frequently asked questions

What are customer unmet needs? Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products or services don't fulfil. They can range from minor frustrations (a feature that's hard to find) to major pain points (a category that doesn't serve a user group well). Identifying them is essential for innovation and competitive differentiation.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. # Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

This does not undermine the dual-path framework; instead, it suggests that structural readiness is a necessary precondition for widespread adoption, even in constraint-driven contexts. Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

Title: Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. Long-Term Institutional Adoption
# Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. The October 2025 liquidity crisis exposed deep flaws in the crypto ecosystem. Regulatory shifts in Asia, coupled with attacks on decentralized protocols, triggered a cascade of liquidations. Markets fragmented across exchanges, with no cross-venue arbitrage to stabilize prices during volatility. Ownership concentration among whales and early investors exacerbated panic selling, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of price drops and forced liquidations. Unlike traditional markets, crypto lacks robust derivatives or insurance mechanisms to absorb shocks. This fragility was compounded by off-chain settlement processes and operational risks tied to decentralized infrastructure according to analysis. Data from CoinLaw.io reveals that 78% of institutional investors now employ formal risk management frameworks, with 53% conducting liquidity stress tests-a stark contrast to 2023, when only 54% had such protocols. ### Institutional Adoption: A Counterweight to Chaos. Despite these risks, institutional participation has introduced stabilizing forces. By 2025, 59% of surveyed institutions allocated at least 10% of their portfolios to digital assets, a shift from speculative bets to strategic integration. Infrastructure innovations are addressing liquidity gaps. The impact of institutional adoption is evident in Bitcoin's reduced volatility. Annualized volatility dropped by 75% by mid-2025, driven by deeper liquidity and a "strong hands" effect, where large investors resist panic selling. ### The Path Forward: Balancing Risks and Resilience. While institutional adoption mitigates some risks, challenges persist. Cybersecurity threats remain unaddressed, and the pro-cyclical nature of crypto liquidity ensures future shocks. However, the market's trajectory suggests a path toward resilience. By 2035, the crypto market is projected to grow from $3.7 billion to $12.1 billion at a 12.6% CAGR, driven by institutional infrastructure and DeFi innovation. Exchange platforms, now accounting for 38.6% of market revenue, are integrating real-time order matching and API-based systems to bolster trust. The crypto market's resilience hinges on its ability to reconcile structural risks with institutional adoption. While liquidity shocks like the October 2025 crash underscore inherent fragility, the rise of institutional-grade infrastructure and risk management frameworks signals a maturing ecosystem. Investors must navigate this duality: embracing the long-term potential of crypto while hedging against its cyclical vulnerabilities.

results.title: Crypto Adoption in Emerging Markets Poses Risks to Financial Resilience: Moody's
results.snippet:
Jamie Crawley

1 min read

 MCO
 DX-Y.NYB

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent.

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. [...] Moody's also highlighted how increased ownership of cryptocurrency has been concentrated in emerging markets, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa and parts of Latin America. Here, adoption is often driven by inflationary pressure, currency pressured and limited access to banking services. In contrast, adoption in more advanced economies, adoption is driven by institutional integration and regulatory clarity.

Crypto ownership expanded to an estimated 562 million people by 2024, an increase of 33% from 2023, the report said.

results.title: Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder
results.snippet:
# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. First, it introduces a novel Regulatory Permissiveness Index, which offers a country-level measure of legal clarity and institutional support for digital assets. Exchange rate volatility (β = −0.002, p = 0.9639) and inflation (β = 0.157, p = 0.1379) do not exhibit statistically significant associations with cryptocurrency adoption. This result supports the null hypothesis (H01) for inflation and stands in contrast to the theoretical framing presented earlier, where inflation was posited as a key motivator based on its perceived threat to currency stability. Although cryptocurrencies are often conceptualised as hedges against fiat devaluation, the evidence suggests that monetary instability alone is insufficient to consistently drive adoption across countries. [...] Importantly, the empirical findings reveal that opportunity-related structural factors, such as GDP per capita, internet penetration, and regulatory clarity, exert stronger and more consistent effects on cryptocurrency adoption. Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent.

Pricing artificial intelligence (AI) software is more difficult than it looks, and the issue lies in deciding what to charge for. The global software-as-a-service (SaaS) market was valued at $209.95 billion in 2024, yet many SaaS founders have pricing strategies built from the subscription era. Those strategies don’t work for AI products because the value customers get and the costs you incur scale with usage in ways that flat pricing can’t absorb.

Below, we’ll cover five AI SaaS pricing models, the weaknesses of each as you scale, and how to work through the decision for your product.

Highlights

   A common AI SaaS pricing mistake is charging per seat when value scales with usage; it creates a margin problem that compounds as your best customers grow. [...] ### Hybrid (subscription plus usage)

A base fee covers a defined amount of usage, and any consumption above that accrues variable charges. Mature AI SaaS products use this model because it gives customers a predictable floor and protects your business against high-volume users that would otherwise compress margins.

### Seat-based

Charging per user makes sense when value scales with adoption across a team. It benefits AI specifically if your costs are driven by compute rather than users. If your heaviest users pay the same as your lightest, that’s a margin problem that compounds as you grow.

### Outcome-based [...] ## How does AI change SaaS pricing?

Traditional SaaS pricing relies on flat subscriptions or per-seat licenses, models in which customers pay a fixed fee tied to the number of users. AI disrupts this model because value and cost scale with usage. When a product generates outputs (e.g., summaries, code, analyses), the value to the customer usually grows with the volume and quality of those outputs, not the number of employees logged in. At the same time, the provider incurs marginal costs each time the AI runs an inference. A heavy user who generates thousands of outputs per day can create far more infrastructure cost than a casual user, even if both occupy one “seat.”

results.snippet:
## What Is Customer Acquisition Cost and How Do You Calculate It?

Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the total amount your business spends to win one new customer. It includes every cost directly associated with bringing in new business: advertising spend, sales team time, marketing tools, content production, events, and any other resource dedicated to converting prospects into customers.

The formula is: Total Sales and Marketing Spend divided by Number of New Customers Acquired equals CAC.

### Customer Acquisition Cost Calculation Example

| Input | Example Value |
 --- |
| Total sales and marketing spend (monthly) | $4,800 |
| New customers acquired during the month | 8 |
| Customer acquisition cost | $4,800 / 8 = $600 per customer | [...] ### Build a Follow-Up System

Generating leads without a reliable follow-up system is one of the most common and costly acquisition mistakes small businesses make. Research published in Harvard Business Review found that businesses responding to leads within one hour are seven times more likely to qualify those leads than those who wait. A CRM with automated reminders and call lists makes consistent follow-up systematic rather than dependent on whoever happens to remember.

### Measure and Optimize

Track CAC by channel, not just in aggregate. Knowing your total CAC is useful. Knowing that referrals produce customers at $150 each while paid search produces them at $900 each is actionable. Review channel performance monthly and reallocate budget toward what is working. [...] ### What Is a Good Customer Acquisition Cost for a Small Business?

It depends on your customer lifetime value. The most widely used benchmark is a 3:1 CLV-to-CAC ratio, each customer should generate at least three times more than they cost to acquire. A ratio below 2:1 signals that acquisition costs are unsustainably high. A ratio above 5:1 may indicate underinvestment in growth. The right CAC target varies by industry, margin, and growth stage.

Title: Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. Long-Term Institutional Adoption
# Crypto Market Resilience Amid Liquidity Shocks: Structural Risks vs. The October 2025 liquidity crisis exposed deep flaws in the crypto ecosystem. Regulatory shifts in Asia, coupled with attacks on decentralized protocols, triggered a cascade of liquidations. Markets fragmented across exchanges, with no cross-venue arbitrage to stabilize prices during volatility. Ownership concentration among whales and early investors exacerbated panic selling, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of price drops and forced liquidations. Unlike traditional markets, crypto lacks robust derivatives or insurance mechanisms to absorb shocks. This fragility was compounded by off-chain settlement processes and operational risks tied to decentralized infrastructure according to analysis. Data from CoinLaw.io reveals that 78% of institutional investors now employ formal risk management frameworks, with 53% conducting liquidity stress tests-a stark contrast to 2023, when only 54% had such protocols. ### Institutional Adoption: A Counterweight to Chaos. Despite these risks, institutional participation has introduced stabilizing forces. By 2025, 59% of surveyed institutions allocated at least 10% of their portfolios to digital assets, a shift from speculative bets to strategic integration. Infrastructure innovations are addressing liquidity gaps. The impact of institutional adoption is evident in Bitcoin's reduced volatility. Annualized volatility dropped by 75% by mid-2025, driven by deeper liquidity and a "strong hands" effect, where large investors resist panic selling. ### The Path Forward: Balancing Risks and Resilience. While institutional adoption mitigates some risks, challenges persist. Cybersecurity threats remain unaddressed, and the pro-cyclical nature of crypto liquidity ensures future shocks. However, the market's trajectory suggests a path toward resilience. By 2035, the crypto market is projected to grow from $3.7 billion to $12.1 billion at a 12.6% CAGR, driven by institutional infrastructure and DeFi innovation. Exchange platforms, now accounting for 38.6% of market revenue, are integrating real-time order matching and API-based systems to bolster trust. The crypto market's resilience hinges on its ability to reconcile structural risks with institutional adoption. While liquidity shocks like the October 2025 crash underscore inherent fragility, the rise of institutional-grade infrastructure and risk management frameworks signals a maturing ecosystem. Investors must navigate this duality: embracing the long-term potential of crypto while hedging against its cyclical vulnerabilities.

## 2.     Overview of the crypto asset market

Crypto assets regularly experience periods of high volatility, with price fluctuations affecting systemically the crypto market. This instability is exacerbated by the use of leveraged derivatives, which can trigger cascading liquidations, but also market concentration due to crypto whales ( 0,004% wallets with more than 1,000 BTC representing 39% of the supply).

Crypto assets regularly experience periods of high volatility, with price fluctuations affecting systemically the crypto market. 

Romain Dalbard

Romain Dalbard, risk manager, 6 Monks [...] Once the liquidation period has been determined, the liquidity discount can be calculated by examining the volatility of each crypto asset. This is estimated using a daily VaR calculation and then extrapolated over the liquidation period. In the development of the VaR model, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed that the daily log-returns of crypto assets do not follow a normal distribution. As a result, the VaR cannot be extrapolated by multiplying the daily VaR by the square root of time. After extensive analysis, 6M's risk management function has concluded that a fat-tailed distribution (i.e. a distribution where the number of observations is greater than the normal distribution in the area away from its central value) is required to model the daily log-returns with an appropriate time [...] Distribution of daily log-returns for the BTC-USD pair from 01/01/2021 to 30/09/2024. A fat-tailed distribution has been calibrated, with a p-value of 25.9% for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. (Photo: 6 Monks)

## 4.     Challenges encountered

Modelling liquidity risk for an asset class as specific as crypto assets presents a number of challenges.

First, access to observable market data is paramount, as liquidity modelling requires accurate, granular and comprehensive data for each crypto asset and exchange platform. Using aggregated data is an attractive approach for a risk manager, but it would not reflect the fund's access to markets or its true liquidation capacity.

# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

Romain Dalbard, risk manager, 6 Monks [...] Once the liquidation period has been determined, the liquidity discount can be calculated by examining the volatility of each crypto asset. This is estimated using a daily VaR calculation and then extrapolated over the liquidation period. In the development of the VaR model, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed that the daily log-returns of crypto assets do not follow a normal distribution. As a result, the VaR cannot be extrapolated by multiplying the daily VaR by the square root of time. After extensive analysis, 6M's risk management function has concluded that a fat-tailed distribution (i.e. a distribution where the number of observations is greater than the normal distribution in the area away from its central value) is required to model the daily log-returns with an appropriate time [...] Distribution of daily log-returns for the BTC-USD pair from 01/01/2021 to 30/09/2024. A base fee covers a defined amount of usage, and any consumption above that accrues variable charges. Mature AI SaaS products use this model because it gives customers a predictable floor and protects your business against high-volume users that would otherwise compress margins.

### Seat-based

Charging per user makes sense when value scales with adoption across a team. It benefits AI specifically if your costs are driven by compute rather than users. If your heaviest users pay the same as your lightest, that’s a margin problem that compounds as you grow.

### Outcome-based [...] ## How does AI change SaaS pricing?

Traditional SaaS pricing relies on flat subscriptions or per-seat licenses, models in which customers pay a fixed fee tied to the number of users. AI disrupts this model because value and cost scale with usage. When a product generates outputs (e.g., summaries, code, analyses), the value to the customer usually grows with the volume and quality of those outputs, not the number of employees logged in. In formal terms, customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the total expenditure needed for a business to acquire one new customer. In the development of the VaR model, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed that the daily log-returns of crypto assets do not follow a normal distribution. As a result, the VaR cannot be extrapolated by multiplying the daily VaR by the square root of time. After extensive analysis, 6M's risk management function has concluded that a fat-tailed distribution (i.e. a distribution where the number of observations is greater than the normal distribution in the area away from its central value) is required to model the daily log-returns with an appropriate time [...] Distribution of daily log-returns for the BTC-USD pair from 01/01/2021 to 30/09/2024. A fat-tailed distribution has been calibrated, with a p-value of 25.9% for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. (Photo: 6 Monks)

First, access to observable market data is paramount, as liquidity modelling requires accurate, granular and comprehensive data for each crypto asset and exchange platform. Using aggregated data is an attractive approach for a risk manager, but it would not reflect the fund's access to markets or its true liquidation capacity.

What's the difference between unmet needs and customer feedback? Feedback is what customers tell you directly, usually in response to a question or a request for a review. Unmet needs are often latent, meaning customers experience them but don't articulate them. Good unmet needs research surfaces both. [...] Unmet needs are the wants and desires that existing products and services don't fulfil. Identifying them is essential for innovation, differentiation, and long-term customer loyalty.
 Empathy is the foundation of unmet needs research. The goal is to view problems from the customer's perspective, not to validate hypotheses you already hold.
 Five research methods work well for uncovering unmet needs: generative research, digital ethnography, customer journey mapping, diary studies, and in-home usage tests (iHUTs).
 A multi-method approach almost always produces richer findings than any single method alone. Initial fieldwork can feed into follow-up interviews and focus groups for deeper exploration.

results.snippet:
# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

Pricing artificial intelligence (AI) software is more difficult than it looks, and the issue lies in deciding what to charge for. The global software-as-a-service (SaaS) market was valued at $209.95 billion in 2024, yet many SaaS founders have pricing strategies built from the subscription era. Those strategies don’t work for AI products because the value customers get and the costs you incur scale with usage in ways that flat pricing can’t absorb.

Below, we’ll cover five AI SaaS pricing models, the weaknesses of each as you scale, and how to work through the decision for your product.

Highlights

   A common AI SaaS pricing mistake is charging per seat when value scales with usage; it creates a margin problem that compounds as your best customers grow. [...] ### Hybrid (subscription plus usage)

A base fee covers a defined amount of usage, and any consumption above that accrues variable charges. Mature AI SaaS products use this model because it gives customers a predictable floor and protects your business against high-volume users that would otherwise compress margins.

### Seat-based

Charging per user makes sense when value scales with adoption across a team. It benefits AI specifically if your costs are driven by compute rather than users. If your heaviest users pay the same as your lightest, that’s a margin problem that compounds as you grow.

### Outcome-based [...] ## How does AI change SaaS pricing?

Traditional SaaS pricing relies on flat subscriptions or per-seat licenses, models in which customers pay a fixed fee tied to the number of users. AI disrupts this model because value and cost scale with usage. When a product generates outputs (e.g., summaries, code, analyses), the value to the customer usually grows with the volume and quality of those outputs, not the number of employees logged in. At the same time, the provider incurs marginal costs each time the AI runs an inference. A heavy user who generates thousands of outputs per day can create far more infrastructure cost than a casual user, even if both occupy one “seat.”

This result supports the null hypothesis (H01) for inflation and stands in contrast to the theoretical framing presented earlier, where inflation was posited as a key motivator based on its perceived threat to currency stability. results.snippet:
# Principles of an Indie Game Bottom Feeder

Moving into indie development? Find an underserved niche audience, "accept what you can't change, be as awesome as you can, charge what you're worth, and stand proud on the ocean floor," writes Spiderweb Software's Jeff Vogel.

Picture of Jeff Vogel

February 9, 2012

Game Developer logo in a gray background | Game Developer

Ever since I founded Spiderweb Software and released my first game in January of 1995, I have been a proud indie game bottom feeder. I have fed and grown fat upon the scraps left behind by the mighty predators above. I have learned well the secret power that writers of indie games can use to actually make a living: We can find a small niche long-abandoned by the big companies, settle into it, and thrive. [...] This is what is important to remember: If you are serving an underserved niche, the neglected gamers who want that sort of game will be thrilled to find you. They will be excited enough to pay a premium price. On the other hand, if you're selling a game in a genre that isn't hugely popular (like turn-based old school RPGs), a low price won't tempt many customers into a purchase, not when there are a million games with a broader appeal for sale on the same page at a lower price.

# We Are The Proud Bottom Feeders. Join Us! [...] Last year, we released Avadon: The Black Fortress HD, our first game for the iPad. Old school, Western-style turn-based RPGs are almost unknown on the platform, so we were serving a classic underserved niche. However, the audience for such games on the iPad was, we guessed, not huge. We decided to sell our game for the princely sum of $9.99. That's a lot on the iPad. We then made what, for our tiny company, was a lot of money.

# Three Trends Shaping The Gaming Industry In 2026

ByChris Hewish,

Forbes Councils Member.

Chris Hewish, Xsolla's Chief Strategy Officer, leads the gaming business engine, offering 700+ payment methods in 200+ regions.

The gaming industry is often described as volatile, powered by hits and highly dependent on platforms. But that framing is starting to feel outdated. Studios are diversifying their distribution channels, and player spending is growing, just in ways that traditional measurement systems are not fully capturing. And AI is reshaping the economics of development, making it faster and more efficient to create new games and keep the classics running.​

## The Rise Of Direct-To-Consumer Sales [...] Gaming is starting to follow that same logic. Major studios are already generating a significant share of revenue through their own direct channels. A key catalyst was the Epic Games v. Apple antitrust case in 2025, which allowed in-app links to external purchasing options, effectively legitimizing what had previously been a workaround.​

With a multichannel sales strategy, studios can reduce their dependence on any single platform, particularly one that may change its rules overnight. At the same time, owning the customer relationship lets them tailor offers and experiences to different player segments.​

Building direct-to-consumer infrastructure requires investment in payments, compliance and customer experience. But in exchange, studios gain something far more valuable: control.​ [...] AI is also helping studios maintain and modernize long-running games. Many of the industry's most successful titles—World of Warcraft, League of Legends, Grand Theft Auto Online—have been on the market for a decade or more. Maintaining these "forever games" and their complex and often outdated codebases can be resource-intensive, especially as original developers move on.​

AI is now helping teams keep these older classics running smoothly. In some cases, this may extend the lifespan of games that would otherwise be retired due to maintenance costs.​

The old model for success—build a hit, ride the platform, repeat—is fading. Studios need to prioritize owning their distribution, knowing their players and using AI as an operational tool while keeping the creative part in human hands.​

Cryptocurrency adoption in emerging markets poses risks to monetary sovereignty and financial resilience, credit ratings giant Moody's Ratings said in a report on Thursday.

The risks are most acute in areas where crypto's use extends beyond investment into savings and remittances, according to the report. Moody's suggests that higher penetration of stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar weaken monetary transmission when it leads to pricing and settlement increasingly occurring outside a market's domestic currency.

Stablecoins are crypto tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, such as a fiat currency, with the U.S. dollar comfortably the most prevalent. Crypto-asset volatility is not a temporary bug that will disappear as markets mature: it is a structural feature. An asset with no cash flows, a highly volatile investor base, liquidity that evaporates under stress, and a valuation entirely dependent on the global liquidity regime will structurally be more volatile than an asset that pays dividends, attracts pension funds, and benefits from bond-market dealers. Understanding this volatility means understanding why crypto cycles are several times more violent than equity cycles, and why they will remain so. [...] 2. Fragmented and procyclical liquidity. Crypto assets trade across dozens of venues (Binance, Coinbase, Bybit, OKX, Kraken, plus DEXs) with fragmented order books. The bid-ask spread on Bitcoin, very tight in normal times on the major venues (Kaiko Research), widened sharply under stress (May 2022, Terra collapse); on altcoins, it becomes wide enough to make rational execution nearly impossible. Liquidity available in normal times disappears precisely when it is needed, and far more than in equity markets, where S&P 500 spreads also widen under stress, but much less. [...] Bitcoin: annualized volatility of at least 60% over 2020–2024 (Bloomberg), several times that of the S&P 500, gold or ten-year Treasuries; Ethereum and the main altcoins are more volatile still. Solana lost most of its value between November 2021 and December 2022, then soared between January 2023 and March 2024. No traditional asset class produces comparable amplitudes. The question is not “why are crypto assets volatile?”: volatility is the logical consequence of their nature. The real question is: which structural mechanisms generate this volatility, and how do those mechanisms interact with the global liquidity cycle?

Highlights

A base fee covers a defined amount of usage, and any consumption above that accrues variable charges. Mature AI SaaS products use this model because it gives customers a predictable floor and protects your business against high-volume users that would otherwise compress margins.

### Seat-based

Charging per user makes sense when value scales with adoption across a team. It benefits AI specifically if your costs are driven by compute rather than users. If your heaviest users pay the same as your lightest, that’s a margin problem that compounds as you grow.

Traditional SaaS pricing relies on flat subscriptions or per-seat licenses, models in which customers pay a fixed fee tied to the number of users. AI disrupts this model because value and cost scale with usage. When a product generates outputs (e.g., summaries, code, analyses), the value to the customer usually grows with the volume and quality of those outputs, not the number of employees logged in. # Recurring Revenue with Digital Products: 5 Models Compared

14 min read

InsightRaider logo

InsightRaider Team

You launched a course. It sold well for two weeks. Then the revenue flatlined. So you launched another product. Same spike, same crash.

That's the revenue roller coaster. And you're stuck on it because you built a one-time-sale business in a subscription world.

The math is brutal: if your average product sells for $49 and you need $10,000/month to live, you need 204 new customers every single month. Miss a launch? Income craters. Get sick for a week? Revenue disappears. [...] Acquisition cost pressure: Acquiring a subscriber often takes about the same effort as acquiring a one-time buyer. But a subscriber who stays can pay you many times more over their lifetime. This means you can spend more on marketing, afford more paid ads, and outcompete creators still running the launch-to-launch game.

## Five Recurring Revenue Models That Work for Digital Products

Not all subscription models are equal. These five fit digital products best, because each one gives buyers a reason to keep paying.

### 1. Membership Sites

How it works: Customers pay monthly or annually for access to an evolving library of content, resources, or training.

Best for: Educators, coaches, and experts with a deep body of knowledge [...] Creators who build recurring revenue sleep better and plan further ahead. Instead of starting each month at $0, they start with last month's subscribers, minus whoever cancelled.

That's not a nice-to-have. That's a fundamentally different business.

## The One-Time Sales Trap

One-time sales aren't inherently bad. They're a great way to validate an idea and generate quick cash. But as a long-term business model, they come with serious structural problems.

The launch dependency cycle: Your revenue is directly tied to how often you launch. No launch, no money. This forces you into a constant content creation grind where you're always building the next thing instead of improving what you already have.

# Three Trends Shaping The Gaming Industry In 2026

ByChris Hewish,

Forbes Councils Member.

Chris Hewish, Xsolla's Chief Strategy Officer, leads the gaming business engine, offering 700+ payment methods in 200+ regions.

The gaming industry is often described as volatile, powered by hits and highly dependent on platforms. But that framing is starting to feel outdated. Studios are diversifying their distribution channels, and player spending is growing, just in ways that traditional measurement systems are not fully capturing. And AI is reshaping the economics of development, making it faster and more efficient to create new games and keep the classics running.​

## The Rise Of Direct-To-Consumer Sales [...] Gaming is starting to follow that same logic. Major studios are already generating a significant share of revenue through their own direct channels. A key catalyst was the Epic Games v. Apple antitrust case in 2025, which allowed in-app links to external purchasing options, effectively legitimizing what had previously been a workaround.​

With a multichannel sales strategy, studios can reduce their dependence on any single platform, particularly one that may change its rules overnight. At the same time, owning the customer relationship lets them tailor offers and experiences to different player segments.​

Building direct-to-consumer infrastructure requires investment in payments, compliance and customer experience. But in exchange, studios gain something far more valuable: control.​ [...] AI is also helping studios maintain and modernize long-running games. Many of the industry's most successful titles—World of Warcraft, League of Legends, Grand Theft Auto Online—have been on the market for a decade or more. Maintaining these "forever games" and their complex and often outdated codebases can be resource-intensive, especially as original developers move on.​

AI is now helping teams keep these older classics running smoothly. In some cases, this may extend the lifespan of games that would otherwise be retired due to maintenance costs.​

The old model for success—build a hit, ride the platform, repeat—is fading. Studios need to prioritize owning their distribution, knowing their players and using AI as an operational tool while keeping the creative part in human hands.​

Pricing artificial intelligence (AI) software is more difficult than it looks, and the issue lies in deciding what to charge for. The global software-as-a-service (SaaS) market was valued at $209.95 billion in 2024, yet many SaaS founders have pricing strategies built from the subscription era.
